title: Where Does the Sky End?
question: How is Earth's atmosphere arranged from the ground up to space?
hook: There is no line in the sky where air stops and space begins, so where do scientists draw it?
idea: The atmosphere thins with height through distinct layers, with most of its mass near the ground and no definite outer edge.

beats.prompt: Put these heights in order, from lowest to highest.
items: The height with three-quarters of the air's mass below it
The outer reach of the far-ultraviolet geocorona
beats.explain: Three-quarters of the mass lies within about 11 km, the Kármán line is at 100 km, the exobase sits at about 500 to 1,000 km, and the geocorona reaches at least 100,000 km.

beats.prompt: You collect dry air samples at 10 km and at 70 km altitude. How do the relative amounts of the gases compare?

choices.label: They are the same in both
Lighter gases dominate higher up
choices.feedback: That happens only above the mixing zone, starting around 80 to 120 km.

choices.label: Heavier gases dominate higher up
choices.feedback: Turbulence keeps the gases evenly mixed below about 100 km, so nothing is sorted by weight.

beats.explain: Up to about 100 km, turbulence mixes the gases so that their relative concentrations remain the same.

beats.prompt: Sort each gas into its group.
beats.explain: Nitrogen, oxygen and argon are the three major constituents; the remaining gases, including greenhouse gases like carbon dioxide, methane and ozone, are trace gases.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning is wrong; which?
steps: Air gets thinner the higher you go
There is no definite boundary between air and space
So the edge of space is set by convention
That convention, the Kármán line, sits at 11 km
beats.explain: The Kármán line is at 100 km; 11 km is roughly the height below which three-quarters of the atmosphere's mass lies.
